lecons.titre: Moving up in your job (1 to 6)
lecons.html:
1. Your job is not a prison

Many people see their work as something to be endured: you go because the bills have to be paid, and you wait for the end of the month, or retirement. The Bible sees it differently. Joseph, a slave in Potiphar’s house, worked so well that his master entrusted everything to him (Genesis 39:2-4). Daniel distinguished himself above all the officials, because an excellent spirit was in him (Daniel 6:3). “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings” (Proverbs 22:29).

Your job is a place of learning and a springboard. You receive a salary there, but also skills, relationships and a reputation. Well used, it prepares you for more important positions, or for something else. Paul writes: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

2. Where am I, where am I going?

You do not move up by chance. Before asking for anything, take stock: take a sheet of paper and answer honestly. What do you do well? Ask two colleagues or friends what they see as good in you. What are you missing for the position above yours? What does your employer really pay for, that is, which results matter to him, what makes him earn or save money? Where do you want to be in a year, in three years? And what holds you back: fear, lack of training, wrong contacts? You will fill in the sheet at the end of this chapter.

3. Becoming more valuable

An employer raises and promotes those who bring him more than they cost him. To become more valuable, there are six areas to work on.

Reliability

This is the foundation. Arriving on time, keeping your word, finishing what you started, telling the truth even when it is uncomfortable. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). Without this, the other qualities are worth nothing.

Competence

Learn constantly, and set yourself one new skill per year. Office tools (word processing, spreadsheet, email) open many positions to those who master them. A foreign language, especially English, too. Communication counts just as much: writing clearly, speaking in public, leading a meeting. Think of short training courses, degrees and certificates in your field. And look for a mentor, someone more advanced than you who agrees to advise you.

Solutions

Do not come only with problems. Come with a problem and a proposal. Whoever solves difficulties quickly becomes indispensable.

Visible results

Do your work, and keep track of what succeeded, with figures: “I reduced delivery delays by 20%”, “I found three new clients”. Note them in a notebook: you will need them the day you ask for a raise. Without boasting, make your work visible: a clear report, a summary to your boss.

Relationships

No one advances alone. Be kind to everyone, from the guard to the director. Help your colleagues, learn people’s names. Positions are often given to those we know and trust. “Two are better than one” (Ecclesiastes 4:9).

Responsibility

Volunteer for the difficult tasks, the ones others do not want. You will learn faster there, and your courage will be noticed. Take on responsibilities before you are given the title.

4. Talking about money with your employer

Asking for a raise or a promotion is frightening. This fear is normal, and it decreases when you prepare.

Before

Gather your results for the year, with figures. Find out what people doing the same work earn elsewhere: talk to people in your sector. Decide on your precise request: a sum, a position, paid training. Choose the right moment, after a success or at the end of the year, when your boss is available. Not in the middle of a crisis, nor in a fit of anger.

During

Ask for an appointment: do not do it in a hallway. Stay calm and respectful, and begin by thanking. Present your results, then your request, keeping it clear and short. Then listen to the answer. Do not threaten to leave, unless you are truly ready to do so.

A sentence to begin: “Thank you for seeing me. This year, I (result 1) and (result 2). I would like to take on more responsibilities. I would like to talk about my advancement and my pay.”

After

If the answer is yes, ask for it in writing and thank him. If it is no, or “not now”, ask what must be done to get a yes, and on what date you will talk about it again. Note the answer, and the date of any promise.

5. Knowing your contract and your payslip

Demand a written contract. A job without a contract leaves you without protection. We saw in part V (“Before signing”) how to read a written contract and what it must contain. Keep it in a safe place.

Also understand your payslip. The gross salary is the starting sum, the net salary is what you receive, after contributions (social security, taxes). These contributions also prepare your retirement and your rights. Know your benefits: bonuses, transport, housing, health coverage. They are part of your pay, and a position with a lower salary but good benefits can be worth more. Keep your papers, contract, payslips, certificates: they will serve you for a loan application, a job change or retirement. And find out about your rights: the Labor Code protects you, and in case of a serious problem, the labor inspectorate can guide you.

If you work for the State: advancement follows precise rules (steps, grades, competitive exams). Know them, keep your file up to date and prepare for professional exams. Many promotions are lost for lack of a file, not for lack of merit.

6. The paths to move up

The pathWhat it isGood to know
PromotionMoving up in the same company: team leader, manager, director.The fastest if your employer knows you. Training or an exam is often needed.
Change of positionMoving to another department or another function in the same company.Lets you learn something else without losing seniority.
Change of employerLeaving for another company, for a higher position or salary.Can raise the salary faster. It must be prepared and not done in a fit of anger.
Working for yourselfBecoming independent, a consultant, or starting a business.More freedom, more risks. To be prepared alongside the job (see part VI).

lecons.titre: Moving up in your job (7 to 11)
lecons.html:
7. When to change employers

Staying too long in the same place can stop your progress. Ask yourself the question of leaving when you have learned nothing for a long time, when there is no prospect of advancement despite your efforts and requests, or when your salary is clearly below the market and they refuse to talk about it. And above all when you are asked to do something dishonest: falsify figures, accept a bribe, lie to a client. Daniel preferred the lions’ den to unfaithfulness (Daniel 6).

To do it well, look before leaving. Do not resign without having another solution, unless your safety or your conscience is in danger. Prepare your CV and your interview as we saw in part V (“An honest CV and a short letter”, “The interview”), adding your figures. And never speak ill of your former employer. Finally, respect your notice period and leave your work in order. You will need good references one day.

8. Keep your integrity

The higher you go, the more temptations grow: a bribe to help a client, a small embezzlement, company time or equipment used for yourself. “The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them.” (Prov 11:3) A promotion obtained by dishonest means does not last. A clean reputation, on the other hand, is a capital that does not run out.

9. Your salary is not your ceiling

A salary has a limit. To create wealth, you sooner or later need other sources of income. A skill can be sold outside the job: advice, training, small services, sales. But be careful. Read your contract, because some forbid having another activity or working for a competitor. Do not work for your personal activity during the employer’s hours, and do not use his equipment. And do not endanger the job that feeds you as long as the other activity does not bring in enough. We will see in the next part how to do this without breaking what you live on.

10. When the salary rises, do not spend more

Here is a known trap: you earn more, so you spend more. The bigger house, the better phone, the outings. After a year, you earn more, but you do not have a franc more. The rule is as follows:

When my salary rises, I first set aside at least half of the raise. I put it into savings, into paying off a debt, or into an investment. I live on the rest.

The people who build wealth are not always those who earn the most. They are those who keep the most.

11. An example (invented story)

Marie is a secretary in a distribution company. After three years, her salary has not moved. She decides to act.

She takes a spreadsheet course one evening a week, which she pays for from her savings. She offers her boss to follow up the clients’ invoices, which were often forgotten. In a few months, late payments go down. She notes the figures.

After eighteen months, she asks for an appointment. She presents her results and asks for the position of management assistant. Her boss agrees, with a raise. Marie sets half of the raise aside from the first month.

She keeps learning, and three years later, she is head of administration. (The figures are there just to give an example.)

To sum up

Your job is a springboard, not a prison. Become more valuable through your reliability, your skills, your solutions, your results, your relationships and your responsibilities. Prepare your request for a raise with figures and the right moment, demand a written contract and understand your payslip. If you want to leave, look elsewhere first, never in a fit of anger. Keep your integrity: it sometimes costs, but it always protects. And when the salary rises, save at least half of the raise.

lecons.titre: Changing careers without breaking the chain (1 to 3)
lecons.html:
1. One path taken, another calling

Many people took a path that was not the one they had planned. A training chosen out of necessity, a job found by chance, a trade learned because they had to live. With time, this path has become a reality: it pays the bills, it feeds the family. And yet, deep down, something pulls elsewhere. A gift not being used. A calling you do not dare listen to. An activity you dream of.

If this is your case, you are not making a mistake. Your current path is not an error: it formed you, it gives you income and relationships. The real question is this: how to move toward the other path without destroying what you live on today?

The Bible gives us examples. Paul proclaimed the Gospel, but he also made tents to support himself (Acts 18:3; Acts 20:34). David kept the flocks before reigning. Moses was a shepherd for forty years before being sent. Jesus himself was a carpenter. God does not despise “the day of small things” (Zechariah 4:10). He often prepares through a path that looks like a detour.

2. Is it really a calling, or tiredness?

Before any change, check that your desire is solid. You can want to change because you are tired of your boss, or because another activity looks easy from afar. That is not a calling, it is an escape. Ask yourself a few questions. Is this desire old? Has it been coming back for years, or was it born last week? Are you running toward something, or are you fleeing something? Are there already proofs: people asking for your help in this field, results, a first payment even if modest? Are you ready to work hard, including on the parts you do not like? And have you prayed and asked for advice? “Where there is no counsel, plans fail, but in a multitude of counselors they are established” (Proverbs 15:22). Talk to mature people who know this field and who tell you the truth.

And remember: not everyone is called to change careers. Sometimes, the calling is exercised within the current job, or alongside it, in the evening and on weekends, or in volunteer service. The comfort of a well-paying job is not proof that you are called to it, but neither is it proof of the opposite.

3. A bridge, not a leap

Imagine you want to cross a river. You can jump. If you succeed, it is quickly done, but if you miss, you fall into the water, with the whole family. Or you can build a bridge: it takes more time, but you keep one foot on the bank as long as the other side is not safe.

The bridge rule: you leave one source of income only when another can replace it.

A gentle career change goes through four stages.

StageIndicative durationWhat you do
1. Prepare3 to 6 monthsClarify what I want to do. Learn. Talk to people in the trade. Build my emergency savings. Talk to my family.
2. Test on a small scale6 to 12 monthsPractice in the evening or on weekends. Find my first clients. Measure what it earns and what it costs me in time.
3. Grow1 to 2 yearsIncrease clients and income. Learn to manage. Improve what I offer.
4. DecideWhen the criteria are metGo part-time, leave the job, keep both, or hire someone to help me.

These durations are benchmarks: everyone moves at his own pace.

When can I leave my job?

Here are five criteria that I propose, and it is better that all of them be met. First, the new activity earns regularly, for at least six months, and at least half of your salary. Second, you have an emergency savings of at least six months of your minimum to live on. Third, you have no heavy debt that depends on your salary. Fourth, your spouse and your family are informed and in agreement. Finally, you have real clients, not just ideas. These figures can be adjusted to your situation, but never leave on a whim.

lecons.titre: Changing careers without breaking the chain (4 to 10)
lecons.html:
4. Training without stopping everything

You do not need to leave your job to learn a new trade. There are evening or weekend courses, in person or remote. There are short training courses and certificates, often more useful than a long degree. There is learning from a professional: offer to help a few hours a week, even for free at the beginning. There is volunteering, in an association or in the Church, to practice and make yourself known. And there are books, videos, and exchanges with people who already do what you want to do. Pay for the training with your project savings, not with a loan. If it leads you to an income, it will have been a good investment.

5. Testing before committing

The biggest losses come from those who buy the machine, rent the premises and order the stock before having a single client. Test small first. Find three people willing to pay, even a little, for what you offer: the real test is that someone pays. Start with what you have, a phone, a table, a few tools, without borrowing. Note everything: how much you earned, how many hours it took, what clients said. Adjust the price, the way of doing things, the place, and keep what works. And do not multiply projects: one test at a time.

Warning. Do not go into debt to launch an activity that has never earned a franc. An idea that has never been paid for by a client is still a dream, not a project.

6. Making the two live together

Running a job and an activity at the same time is difficult. Here is how to hold on.

For time, decide on a fixed number of hours per week, for example ten, at precise times, and write them in your schedule. For energy, protect your rest, your family and your life with God: “The Sabbath was made for man” (Mark 2:27). Exhaustion destroys both activities. For the contract, read the part that speaks of other activities, competition and conflicts of interest. If needed, inform your employer or ask for his agreement. Never work for your activity on the employer’s time or with his equipment.

Do not neglect your current job: it is what feeds you, and a good reputation there is an asset for what comes next. Explain to your family what you are doing and why, and plan time for them. A family that understands supports you, a family left aside ends up holding you back. Finally, for money, open a separate account for the activity as soon as possible, and do not mix it with your expenses.

7. Turning the two into wealth

Here is good news: you do not have to choose between your two paths as if they were opposed. Often, the combination of the two is what makes you unique. Many people know how to do one thing. Few know how to do both. This rarity has value.

The pathWhat it isExample
Crossing the two skillsUsing both trades in a single activity.A nurse who trains families and churches in first aid. An accountant who helps small shopkeepers keep their books.
Selling the job’s expertiseOffering clients, outside the job, what you know how to do (advice, training, service), without conflicting with your employer.A teacher who gives private lessons. A technician who does repairs on weekends.
Two sources of incomeKeeping the job, and growing the activity alongside, for a long time.An employee who sells processed products. A civil servant who farms a field.
Turning the activity into a businessWhen the activity grows, giving it a status, rules, employees.See part VII, on business management.
Choosing a partnerTeaming up with someone whose skill complements yours: one keeps his job, the other devotes himself to the activity.A technician and a salesperson who launch a workshop together.

8. Mistakes to avoid

The same mistakes are always seen. Resigning on a whim, without savings or clients. Launching by going into debt, before having tested. Spreading yourself across three or four projects at once. Neglecting the current job, and losing both security and reputation. Looking for perfection before starting, when it is better to start small and adjust. Keeping your project secret from everyone, when you need advisers. Ignoring your family in the decision. And confusing dream and plan: a plan has dates, figures and first actions.

9. If you really must leave your job

Sometimes, after the test and growth stage, the moment comes to leave. Do it cleanly. Prepare a transition budget: six to twelve months of minimum to live on, in savings, and reduce your expenses before leaving, not after. Ask whether gentle options exist, part-time, unpaid leave, secondment for the State: they keep the door open.

Respect your notice period, hand over your work, stay on good terms. You may need them one day, as clients, as partners or as references. Think of your protection: health insurance, retirement contributions, which are no longer paid automatically when you no longer have a salary. And keep a plan B: what will you do if the activity is slow to earn?

10. An example (invented story)

Nadège is a nurse in a health center. She loves her trade, but she has always dreamed of turning the fruits of her region into juices and jams. She does not dare leave a secure salary.

Stage 1 (4 months). She takes a weekend course on fruit processing. She sets aside three months of minimum to live on. She talks to her husband, who encourages her.

Stage 2 (10 months). Every Saturday, she produces a small quantity at home. She sells to her colleagues and at church. She notes her sales, her costs and her hours. She adjusts her recipes and her price.

Stage 3 (a year and a half). The activity now earns half of her salary. She has real clients, who come back. She opens a separate account and makes a first equipment purchase with her earnings.

Stage 4. She asks to go down to three days a week at the health center. She keeps her trade, and she hires a helper to produce. Later, she adds nutrition workshops to her offer, where her two skills meet. (The figures and durations are there just to give an example.)

To sum up

Your current path is not a mistake: it forms you and feeds you. First check that what pulls you elsewhere is a calling and not an escape. Build a bridge rather than jumping: you leave one source of income only when another can replace it. Test small, because the real test is that a client pays, and never go into debt for an idea that has not yet been paid for. Your two skills together are often worth more than each. And if you leave, leave cleanly, with a reserve and a plan B.

Read this first. This text gives management principles and benchmarks on the rules in force in Benin. Tax and administrative rules change: before acting, check with the General Directorate of Taxes, the SME Development Agency, or an accountant.

1. Why manage well?

Many businesses do not close for lack of clients. They close for lack of management: the business’s money gets mixed with the family’s, no one knows how much is being earned, prices are poorly calculated, clients do not pay, and no one knows where the money is anymore.

“Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established;” (Prov 24:3) “Know well the state of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds” (Prov 27:23). Managing is knowing the state of your flock: knowing what you have, what you owe, what you earn. It is also a way of being faithful in small things (Luke 16:10) with what God has entrusted to us.

2. Separating the business’s money from yours

This is rule number one. Many small businesses die because the owner takes from the till “just a little”, for school fees, for a wedding, for an emergency. After a year, nothing is left, and no one knows where the money went.

The business is not your wallet. It has its money, you have yours.

Open a separate account for the business (a bank or microfinance account, and if possible a Mobile Money number reserved for business). Pay yourself a fixed salary each month, even a small one: it is the only money you take from the business for your personal expenses. If you must take anything else, note it, with the date, the amount and the reason: it will be a loan or an advance, to be repaid. Do not lend the till to the family. Help, if you wish, with your salary, not with the business’s money. And do not pay the business’s expenses with your personal money, nor the reverse, unless you note it.

3. Keeping your accounts simply

You do not need an accountant to start. A well-kept notebook is worth more than a tired memory. Keep at least these four documents:

The documentWhat you note in it
The cash journalEvery money coming in and going out: the date, the description, the amount, the balance.
The client registerWho owes you money, how much, since when.
The supplier registerWhom you owe money, how much, by what date.
The stock registerWhat you have in reserve: quantities bought, sold, remaining.

Also keep all the documents: purchase invoices, receipts, delivery notes, filed by month in a folder. Take thirty minutes each week to update your records. A one-month delay quickly becomes a delay impossible to catch up.

Three words to tell apart

The wordWhat it is
TurnoverThe total of your sales. It is not what you earn.
ProfitWhat is left to you when you have paid all the expenses: purchases, rent, transport, salaries, taxes, and your own salary.
Cash flowThe money actually available in the till and in the account today.

Example: you sold 1,000,000 F this month, but your clients paid only 600,000 F. Your turnover is 1,000,000 F, but your cash holds only 600,000 F. And if you must pay 700,000 F of expenses, you are short, even if the business is “profitable”.

4. Calculating your price

Many bosses set their prices by copying their neighbors, or “by eye”. It is dangerous: you can sell a lot and lose money. Here is how to do it.

The cost price

This is what each product or service costs you. There are two kinds of costs. Variable costs change with quantity: raw materials, packaging, transport, commission. Fixed costs are paid even without selling: rent, electricity, phone, salaries, insurance, loan repayment, and your own salary.

The selling price and the margin

Margin on a product = selling price − variable costs. The margin must serve to pay the fixed costs, then to make a profit.

Example (invented figures): a bottle of juice.

Variable costs per bottle: fruit 200 F, bottle 150 F, sugar 50 F, label 25 F, transport 25 F: 450 F.

Fixed costs per month: 60,000 F (rent, electricity, phone, salary).

Selling price: 800 F. Margin per bottle: 800 − 450 = 350 F.

The break-even point (you neither earn nor lose): 60,000 ÷ 350 = about 172 bottles per month. Below that, you lose money. Above it, you earn.

At 600 bottles per month: 600 × 350 − 60,000 = 150,000 F of profit.

Beware of discounts

A 10% reduction on the price seems small. But it does not cut 10% of the margin, it cuts much more. In our example, if you sell at 720 F instead of 800 F, the margin goes from 350 F to 270 F: minus 23%. At 600 bottles, the profit falls from 150,000 F to 102,000 F: minus 32%. Before giving a discount, redo the calculation.

A price is not only a cost plus a margin. It must also take into account what the client is willing to pay and what others do. But never go below your cost price.

5. Cash flow: avoiding running short

A business that earns money can still go bankrupt. Why? Because money goes out before it comes in. You pay suppliers today, but clients pay in a month. If you have not planned for this gap, you are short. A three-month cash flow table helps you see it in advance. Example (invented figures):

Money at the startMoney coming inMoney going outMoney at the end
Month 1100,000300,000350,00050,000
Month 250,000200,000320,000− 70,000
Month 3− 70,000600,000330,000200,000

Over three months, the business earns 100,000 F. But in month 2, 70,000 F is missing. If you had seen it in advance, you could have asked for a deposit, delayed a purchase or negotiated a delay with a supplier.

To protect your cash flow, ask for a deposit, for example 30% to 50%, before starting a job or delivering a big order. Set short payment terms, and respect those of your own suppliers. Follow up with clients who are late (we come to that). Negotiate delays with your suppliers. Avoid big stocks that sit idle, because it is money tied up. And keep a reserve of at least one to three months of fixed expenses.

lecons.titre: Invoicing: quote, invoice, VAT and standardized invoice
lecons.html:
6. Invoicing: quote, invoice and other documents

“A false balance is an abomination to Yahweh, but accurate weights are his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). A clear and honest invoice is an accurate weight. It protects the client, it protects you, and it gets you paid.

The different documents

The documentWhat it is for
The quoteA price offer, before the work. The client signs it to say “agreed”. State the period of validity.
The proforma invoiceA provisional document that looks like an invoice. It is used for example for a financing request, a payment before delivery, or customs clearance. It is not a real invoice: it does not yet ask for payment.
The purchase orderThe document by which the client confirms his order.
The delivery noteThe proof that you delivered. The client signs it on receipt.
The invoiceThe official document that asks for payment, after the delivery or the work.
The receiptThe proof that the client has paid.
The credit noteA document that cancels or corrects an invoice: returned product, price error.
The account statementThe list of all of a client’s invoices and what remains to be paid.

What an invoice must contain

Here is the usual information. The exact list may be specified by the tax administration: check it. An invoice bears the word “Invoice” and a unique number, which follows an order with no gap (001, 002, 003…), as well as the date. It gives your identity: business name, address, phone, RCCM number, IFU number (unique tax identifier), and that of the client, with his IFU if it is a business. Each product or service is described there, with the quantity and the unit price excluding tax. It shows the total, and the VAT if you are authorized to charge it; otherwise, a mention indicates your regime. It specifies the payment terms: deadline, payment method (transfer, Mobile Money, cash) and details for paying. Finally, it bears your signature or your stamp.

The standardized invoice

In Benin, the tax administration (the DGI) has set up the standardized invoice. It is produced by a certified electronic machine (the MECeF, today also in an online version, the e-MECeF). It also contains security elements: the machine’s number, a signature and an electronic code. This makes it possible to verify each invoice.

It is mandatory for businesses subject to VAT. In principle, the law imposes it on all businesses, large or small. In practice, large businesses and administrations often require a standardized invoice from their suppliers, even when these are small. If you want to work with them, you will need it. Ask the DGI about the current conditions.

VAT: what you need to know

VAT (value-added tax) is 18% in Benin. It is paid by the client, and you pass it on to the State. It is not your money. It is not part of your profit.

Example: you sell for 100,000 F excluding tax. With VAT, the client pays 100,000 + 18,000 = 118,000 F. The 18,000 F is passed on to the State.

Not everyone can charge VAT. According to the published rules, a business subject to the TPS (see below) that has not chosen the real regime cannot charge VAT. Businesses that exceed 50 million CFA francs of turnover per year, or that have chosen the real regime, can charge it. Never charge VAT if you are not entitled to. Have your situation confirmed by an accountant or by the DGI.

Example of an invoice

DescriptionQuantityUnit priceTotal
Pineapple juice, 1-liter bottle401,500 F60,000 F
Mango jam, 250 g jar301,200 F36,000 F
Total96,000 F
Deposit already received (on the 5th of the month)− 30,000 F
Balance to pay66,000 F

Invoice no. 014, issued on the 20th of the month, for Hôtel Les Palmiers. Your name, your address, your RCCM and your IFU, those of the client, the mention “VAT not applicable” if you are under the TPS, and the payment terms (“Payment within fifteen days, by transfer or Mobile Money to…”) come in addition.

The ways of invoicing

The typeWhen to use itExample
Cash invoiceThe client pays right away.A restaurant, a shop.
Term invoiceThe client pays later, on a fixed date (15, 30 days).A delivery to a business.
Deposit invoiceTo ask for part of the price before the work.A carpenter, before buying the wood.
Progress invoiceA large job in stages: you invoice according to progress.A construction site, an installation.
Recurring invoiceA service that repeats: you invoice on a fixed date.Monthly maintenance, a subscription.
Flat-rate invoiceOne overall price for the whole.A complete service at a single price.
Detailed invoiceThe detail of each line.A sale with several products.

Good habits

Invoice right away, on the day of delivery or the end of the work: an invoice sent late is paid late. Number your invoices in order, without skipping any. Keep a copy of each and file them: the administration may ask you for them, and the rule is to keep them for many years. Use templates, a book of numbered invoices, a template on a computer or phone, or the invoicing tool provided by the DGI. And send the invoice by a means that leaves a trace: mail handed over against signature, email, or message.

Never make a false invoice, nor a “favor invoice” for a friend, nor an invoice with an inflated price. It is fraud. It can ruin you, and it dishonors the name of Christ.

lecons.titre: Getting paid, formalizing and steering your business
lecons.html:
7. Getting paid

Issuing an invoice is not enough: the client must pay. A client who does not pay is free work.

Before selling

Agree on the terms in writing: price, payment date, deposit. A signed quote is enough. Find out about the client: does he pay on time? Ask those who have already worked with him. Start small with a new client, and increase the credit if he pays well. And ask for a deposit for big orders.

When the client is late

WhenWhat you do
A few days before the due dateA friendly reminder: “Hello, invoice no. 014 is due on the 5th. Thank you!”
The next dayA polite message: “We have not yet received the payment. Can you confirm the date?”
One week laterA phone call. Ask for a precise date. Note what is promised.
Fifteen days laterA firm written letter, with the amount due and the deadline. Keep a copy.
One month laterA last letter (formal notice). Stop delivering. Seek advice from a lawyer or a bailiff.

The law provides a simple procedure to recover a clear debt, called an “order to pay.” A lawyer or a bailiff can explain how to use it. Always keep the quote, purchase order, delivery note, invoice and messages: they are your proof.

Stay polite, firm and regular. Do not threaten, do not get angry, do not talk about the client to others. And pay your own suppliers and employees on time: “The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning” (Leviticus 19:13).

8. Formalizing and paying your taxes

Many businesses stay in the informal sector out of fear of taxes. Yet the formal business has real advantages: access to credit and bank accounts, the ability to work with large businesses and administrations, legal protection, credibility. The State offers simple regimes for small businesses.

The usual steps: the RCCM (trade and personal property credit register), which registers your activity; the IFU (unique tax identifier), your identity number for taxes; the professional card, when it is required for your activity; and the choice of a status, sole proprietorship or a company such as the SARL. Company law is that of OHADA, and the company protects your personal assets better.

Benin also offers a very simple status, the “entrepreneur” status. It is free and open to anyone who carries out a commercial, craft or farming activity. It comes with a simpler tax, the Synthetic Professional Tax (TPS), which applies to small businesses whose annual turnover is below 50 million CFA francs. Above that, you move to the real regime, with VAT and tax on profits.

Counters exist to help you: the SME Development Agency and the one-stop counters for business formalization. Ask there for the list of documents, costs and current deadlines, because they may change. And pay what you owe: “Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes” (Romans 13:7). Honest accounts allow a business to grow without fearing inspection.

9. Employees and partners

For each employee, make a written contract: tasks, salary, hours, duration. Pay on the planned date, in full, declare your employees and pay the social contributions that fall to you. Set clear rules, known to all. And between partners, also put an agreement in writing: who brings what, who does what, how profits are shared, how one can leave. Partnerships without paper often end badly, even between friends or between brothers.

10. Steering your business every month

Once a month, take one hour to look at six figures: the month’s sales, compared with the previous month; the margin, that is, what is left after variable costs; fixed expenses; the month’s profit; cash flow, the money actually available; and unpaid invoices, that is, the clients who owe you money and for how long. If a figure worries you, look for the cause and act that same month, without waiting for the end of the year.

11. Frequent mistakes

They are almost always the same: mixing the business’s money and your own; not writing down your sales and expenses; setting prices without calculating; giving credit without follow-up, without a deposit, without a limit; making big stocks or big purchases before having sold; forgetting your own expenses (rent, salary, taxes); believing that turnover means profit; staying in the informal sector and losing big clients and credit; and partnering without paper.

12. An example (invented story)

Jean is a carpenter. His clients love him, he works a lot, but he never has any money. He does not know how much he earns. He takes from the till for the family’s needs. He sets his prices by eye, and many clients pay “next month”.

An accountant friend suggests a few changes. Jean opens an account reserved for the workshop and sets himself a salary. He keeps a cash notebook. He calculates the cost price of a table and a wardrobe, and discovers that he was losing money on the wardrobes. He raises his price, and asks for a 50% deposit at the order.

He issues quotes and numbered invoices, and politely follows up with those who are late. He then takes the steps to formalize. A year later, a large company orders desks from him. It requires a standardized invoice, which he can now produce. (Invented story, just to give an example.)

To sum up

Separate the business’s money from your own, and pay yourself a salary. Write everything down: a cash notebook is worth more than memory. Calculate your prices with variable costs, fixed costs, margin and break-even point, and do not forget that turnover, profit and cash flow are not the same thing. Invoice quickly, clearly, in order, and ask for a deposit. In Benin, find out about the standardized invoice and VAT, and do not charge VAT you are not entitled to. Follow up with clients methodically and politely, and keep your proof. Finally, formalize your activity, and pay what you owe.

lecons.titre: Investing (1 to 4): understanding before placing your money
lecons.html:
Read this first. This text gives general principles for learning. It is not personalized advice. No investment is guaranteed: you can lose part of your money, or all of it. Rules, rates and fees change: always check them before acting.

1. What is investing?

Investing is putting money today into something that can produce more tomorrow. It can pay in two ways. Either through regular income: interest, rent, a dividend (a share of a business’s profits), the sales of a harvest. Or through a rise in value: what you bought is worth more when you resell it, land, a share.

You must not confuse investing and speculating. Whoever invests understands what produces the money: a business that sells, a house that is rented, a field that yields harvests. Whoever speculates only bets that the price will rise, like gambling. The first builds. The second plays.

Jesus tells the parable of the talents: the master expects his servants to make fruitful what he entrusted to them (Matthew 25:14-30). Investing is therefore legitimate. But the Bible also asks us for patience: “Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away, but he who gathers by hand makes it grow” (Proverbs 13:11).

2. Before investing: putting your house in order

You do not invest with just any money, nor in just any situation. Before investing a single franc, check this. You no longer have expensive debt (high-rate loan, overdraft, private lender): paying off a debt at 2% a month pays more than any serious investment. You have an emergency savings of at least three months of minimum to live on, and the basic insurances (health, vehicle if you have one). You have a goal and a duration: for what, and in how long you will need this money. And you invest only money you will not need for several years.

Golden rule: never invest borrowed money, nor money you need for food, for rent or for school fees.

3. The laws of investing

Three questions for each investment

QuestionWhat it means
How much can it earn? (the return)The possible gain, as a percentage per year.
How much can I lose? (the risk)The part of my money that I can lose, or the chance that it happens.
Can I get my money back quickly? (liquidity)If I need the money tomorrow, can I withdraw it without losing? A house or a piece of land cannot be sold in a week.

Return and risk go together

The more an investment promises to earn, the riskier it is. There is no huge and safe gain. Whoever promises you both is lying, or deceiving himself. We will see it later with pyramids.

Do not put all your eggs in one basket

“Give a portion to seven, yes, even to eight; for you don’t know what evil will be on the earth” (Ecclesiastes 11:2). Spread your money across several investments of different nature. If one loses, the others hold. This is called diversifying.

Time works for you

A risky investment over one day is dangerous. The same one, kept ten years, is less so. The more time you have, the more you can bear the bad years. Start early, even with little. Also keep an eye on fees and taxes: an investment that earns 6% but costs 2% in fees leaves you only 4%. Always ask for all the fees, in writing, as well as the taxes to pay.

Understand before buying

If you cannot explain in a few simple sentences how this investment produces money, do not put a franc into it.

4. An overview of investments

InvestmentHow it paysRiskMoney recoverable?
Term deposit (bank, approved microfinance)A fixed interest, known in advance.Very low.Locked until the date.
Treasury bills and bonds (the State borrows)An interest set in advance, and the capital returned at the end.Low, but not zero.At the end of the term, or by selling before.
Shares (parts of businesses, on the stock exchange)Dividends, and the value of the share which can rise.High. Prices go up and down.By selling, if a buyer shows up.
Mutual fundsA manager invests the money of many savers.Medium to high, depending on the fund.Often fairly quickly.
LandIt gains value with time.Medium: disputes, poor location.Difficult and slow.
Rental real estateRents, and the value of the property.Medium: unpaid rents, maintenance.Difficult and slow.
Agriculture, livestockThe sale of harvests or animals.High: weather, diseases, prices, theft.At harvest, or at sale.
A business (yours, or a share)The business’s profits.High.Often difficult.
CryptocurrenciesYou hope the price rises.Very high, and unregulated.Possible, but the price can collapse.

lecons.titre: The stock exchange, Treasury bills, land and real estate
lecons.html:
5. The stock exchange: the BRVM

What is a share? What is a bond?

A share is a small piece of a business. When you buy a share, you become the owner of a tiny part of that business. If it makes profits, it can pay part of them to shareholders: this is the dividend. If it does badly, the share price falls, and you can lose.

A bond is a loan that you make to a business or a State. They pay you interest each year, and return your capital at the end. The risk is lower than for a share, because the amounts and dates are set in advance.

The BRVM, the stock exchange of our region

The BRVM (Regional Securities Exchange) is the common stock exchange of the eight countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, including Benin. It is based in Abidjan. Shares and bonds of companies in the region are bought and sold there: banks, telecommunications, energy, industry, and others.

An individual cannot buy directly on the stock exchange. He must go through an approved intermediary, an SGI (management and intermediation company). Here is how it works. You choose an approved SGI: ask to see its approval from the Union’s financial market supervisory authority (the CREPMF), and compare the fees of two or three SGIs. You open a securities account: you sign an agreement and a form, with an ID and other documents that the SGI tells you about. You deposit money in this account, because the BRVM operates on a cash basis: you must have the money before buying. You then place a purchase order through your SGI, specifying which company, how many shares and at what price. Finally, you follow your portfolio through the statements that show your securities, your available money and your transactions.

At each purchase or sale, there are fees: the SGI’s commission, those of the exchange and the custodian, and taxes. Some SGIs also charge custody fees. Ask for the full rate schedule before opening an account, and find out about the tax on dividends.

How to choose your shares well

Understand the business: what does it sell, has it been making money for several years, is it heavily in debt? Look at the dividend: has it been paid regularly for years, and in what amount? Do not follow rumors or “tips” given by a friend, a chat group or a stranger. Diversify among several companies from different sectors. Start small, and invest the same sum each month rather than all at once. Think long term, at least five years, and do not sell in panic when the price falls. And never borrow to buy shares.

Example (invented figures). You buy 10 shares at 5,000 F: 50,000 F. In a good year, the business pays 300 F per share: that makes 3,000 F of dividends, that is 6%. But the price falls to 4,500 F: your 10 shares are now worth 45,000 F. You have lost 5,000 F on paper, and earned 3,000 F of dividends. If you held on, you have not lost 5,000 F. If you sold in panic, you lost it for good.

Prices go up, they go down. That is normal. What counts is what you do when they go down.

Good to know: it happens that you do not immediately find a buyer for your securities, or not at the price you hope for. So place on the stock exchange only money you do not need in the short term.

6. Treasury bills and bonds

The State of Benin regularly borrows money from savers in the region, through the UMOA-Titres agency. It issues bills (short term) and bonds (three, five, seven years…). It pays interest, and returns the capital at the end. It is generally one of the safest investments, because it is the State that repays.

As an example, an issue of November 2024 offered about 5.7% per year for three years, 5.9% for five years and 6% for seven years. Rates change with each issue: this figure is a benchmark, not a promise. This notice also indicated that the income from these securities is exempt from tax for people residing in Benin. Check the conditions of the latest issue.

An individual gets access by going through an approved intermediary: his bank or an SGI. Ask him about the next issues, the term, the rate and the fees. “Safer” does not mean “without risk”: if you resell before the end, the price may be lower, and inflation can eat part of the gain.

7. Land and real estate

Many people invest first in land. It is understandable: you can see it, touch it, it does not disappear. But it is also one of the investments where the most money is lost, for lack of precautions.

Before buying land

Check that the seller is truly the owner. Ask for the documents that prove his right, and have them checked by a notary or with the national agency in charge of state property and land. Make sure the land is not already sold to someone else, that there is no dispute, no opposing family, no mortgage. Visit it, and talk to the neighbors and the neighborhood leaders. Look at the area: floods, access to water, road, urban plan, because some land is in a zone where you cannot build.

Go through a notary, sign a deed, and have the sale registered. Pay by transfer and keep a receipt: no cash without a deed, and never alone. Finally, do not rush. A seller who rushes you is often trying to hide something.

Rental real estate: do the math

Buying a house to rent it out can produce a regular income. But calculate first:

Example (invented figures). A house costs 15,000,000 F. It rents for 100,000 F a month, that is 1,200,000 F a year: 8% of the price. But you must subtract maintenance, taxes, months without a tenant and unpaid rents: say 200,000 F a year. That leaves 1,000,000 F, or about 6.7%. And you must count the time and the worries.

Land alone earns nothing as long as you do not sell it. Everything lies in the difference between the purchase price and the resale price, and in the time it takes.

8. Agriculture and livestock

Producing food is a safe value: people will always eat. It is an excellent investment when well run, and it creates jobs. But the risks are many: rain that fails or is too strong, diseases, theft, the fall in prices at harvest, lack of storage.

To reduce them, start small, on an area or a herd that you master. Get training, and ask advice from those who already succeed in the field. Diversify the crops or the animals, and get insured when it exists (agricultural micro-insurance). Plan the storage and the sale before planting: where and to whom will I sell? Add value by drying, processing, packaging, because you often earn more by processing than by selling raw. And work in a group or cooperative to buy cheaper and sell better.

9. Cryptocurrencies

A cryptocurrency, like bitcoin, is a digital “money” created by private persons, which is exchanged on the Internet. There is no bank or State behind it. Its price depends solely on those who buy and sell it. It can double, then lose half in a few weeks.

The Central Bank of the region took a position in July 2026. Its governor summed it up: “It is not a currency. It is not regulated. So be careful.” He cited three major risks: volatility (you can lose a large part of your capital), the anonymity of transactions often coming from abroad, and hacking. At the time of writing this text, there are not yet any specific rules in the Union, even though a committee is working to define some.

Concretely, you have no protection if you are deceived or hacked: no guarantee fund reimburses you. If you lose your password or your access key, the money is lost forever. Cryptocurrencies are also a prime ground for scams: fake websites, “trading robots” that promise automatic gains, fake advisers, crypto “gifts”. And the word “crypto” is very often used to hide pyramids.

If despite everything you touch them, respect at least these rules: never borrowed money; never the emergency money or the rent money; a very small part of your investments, a sum you accept to lose entirely; never through a stranger; never give your codes to anyone. And if you do not understand, do not touch them.

10. Pyramids and scams

A pyramid (or Ponzi scheme) is a swindle: it promises huge gains. The first participants are paid with the money of the next ones. As long as new people come in, everything seems to work. When they no longer come in, everything collapses. The last ones lose everything, and there are always many of them.

A real example: ICC Services (Benin, 2010). This company and others promised returns of 150 to 200% per quarter. According to the International Monetary Fund, nearly 150,000 people were deceived, for more than 150 billion CFA francs. Merchants, civil servants, whole families lost everything. Some had borrowed to “invest”. The leaders were sentenced to ten years in prison in 2019, but the money was never entirely recovered.

The signs that should alert you

Beware of a huge and quick gain: “double your money in a month”, “30% a month”. Beware of the word “risk-free” or “guaranteed”: no serious investment guarantees a gain. If you are paid to recruit other people, it is a pyramid. If you are pressed to act fast (“the offer ends tomorrow”, “only three places left”), it is a bad sign. There is no visible approval, no office, no clear contract. No one can explain to you where the money comes from: if you do not understand where the gain comes from, it is you who provide it. You are asked to send the money to a personal number by Mobile Money, or in cash. You are shown beautiful cars and big houses as “proof”. And it is a person you trust who advises it: a brother from church, a friend, a relative.

This last point is important. Scammers often use religious trust: they talk about blessing, about “God who multiplies”, or use a prayer group. Faith is shared, but financial trust is verified. “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts” (1 Timothy 6:9). A good brother can be wrong, or have been deceived himself.

The five-question test

Before putting in a franc, ask these five questions. Who is behind this offer? Is he approved, and can I verify it with the authority? How does this investment produce money, and can I explain it to someone? Who guarantees the capital, and what happens if it fails? Can I take my money back whenever I want, and under what conditions? Finally, have I had time to think, to ask for advice and to compare? If even one answer makes you uncomfortable, do not put in a franc.

11. Building your investment plan

An investment plan comes down to a few ideas. Start with the foundation: expensive debts repaid, emergency savings, insurance. Give yourself a goal and a duration: “3,000,000 F in seven years to buy land” is better than “I want to invest money”. Decide on a regular sum each month: investing little but often beats investing a lot only once. Spread your money across several investments. Look at your plan once or twice a year, not every day. And keep your cool: when a price falls, do not sell in panic, and when everything rises and everyone gets carried away, do not rush in.

An example of balance: the three buckets

Here is a simple way to organize the money you invest. The proportions are an example for a cautious person: adapt them to your situation.

The bucketExample shareWhat you put in itIts role
Securityabout 60%Term deposit, Treasury bills and bonds.Protect the capital, keep a solid base.
Growthabout 35%Shares of several companies, land, productive activity, agriculture.Make your money grow in the long term.
Bet5% at mostWhat is very risky (including cryptocurrencies).A sum you accept to lose entirely.

If you are very young, with few responsibilities and a long horizon, you can take a bit more risk. If you are approaching an important need or retirement, take less.

12. Classic mistakes

They are found everywhere. Investing to “make up for it” after a loss is the road to ruin. Going into debt to invest. Following the crowd or a “tip” received by message. Putting everything into a single investment. Selling in panic at the first fall. Ignoring fees and taxes. Not understanding, and trusting someone “because he is a brother”. Forgetting to follow your investments, or on the contrary looking at them every day. And waiting until you have a lot to start: start small.

13. An example (invented story)

Hermann is a teacher. He has repaid his loan, he has three months of minimum to live on in savings, and health insurance. He then decides to invest 30,000 F per month.

He puts 18,000 F into a term deposit and Treasury bonds, 10,000 F into shares of three different companies, bought through an approved SGI whose fees he compared, and 2,000 F into a small bet that he accepts to lose. He notes his investments, rereads them twice a year.

One day, a colleague offers him an “investment” that doubles money in three months. He asks his five questions. No one can tell him where the gain comes from. He refuses. Three months later, the colleague no longer receives anything.

Ten years later, if he has kept the same sum and if his investments have earned an average of 6% a year, his 3,600,000 F of payments will have reached about 4,900,000 F. (Example of a calculation only: the real result may be higher or lower, and nothing is guaranteed.)

To sum up

Investing is understanding what produces money, it is not betting. Before investing, you must be free of expensive debt, have emergency savings and insurance. Gain and risk go together: a huge and safe gain does not exist. Diversify, invest regularly, think long term. On the stock exchange, go through an approved SGI and know all the fees. Before buying land, go to the notary, verify, sign a deed and keep a receipt. Cryptocurrencies are not a currency and are not regulated: extreme caution. And a huge and quick gain is the sign of a scam: religious trust does not excuse you from verifying.

lecons.titre: Rebuilding: being at the bottom is not being finished
lecons.html:
Until now, we have mostly talked about those who are rising: the one looking for a job, the one moving up, the one launching a business. But there is another case, more frequent than we think. It is that of a person who had great means: a business that was doing well, a nice house, employees, a good reputation. Then, at some point in his life, events happened: an important client who no longer pays, a crisis, a dishonest partner, an illness, a fire, a loan that was too heavy, a bad decision. And everything fell. Bankruptcy. Now he is completely at the bottom, with debts, without money, sometimes without a house, and with the eyes of others on him.

If this is your case, or that of someone close to you, this part is written for you. The way back exists, but it does not begin where one thinks. It does not begin with a big project that would erase everything. It begins with a simple and courageous act: sitting down and looking your real situation in the face. Taking stock, counting what you have left, deciding where you want to go, and making a plan to get there. This is what we are going to do together.

1. Being at the bottom is not being finished

The first battle is fought in the head. Whoever falls from high quickly hears, within himself and in the mouths of others, a sentence: “It is over for you.” Reject it. “A righteous man falls seven times, and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). Notice that the verse speaks of falling seven times. The fall is not what makes the difference between people. What does, is getting back up. The prophet says it in one sentence: “when I fall, I will arise” (Micah 7:8).

Job lost everything: his goods, his children, his health. At the end of his story, “Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before” (Job 42:10). This does not mean that every bankruptcy ends with a double. But it shows that God’s story with a man does not stop on the day of his greatest loss.

You must also be honest about the cause. Sometimes, the fall comes from events you did not control. Sometimes, it comes from your mistakes. Most often, a bit of both. Do not accuse yourself of everything, and do not excuse yourself of everything either. We will come back to this.

And take care of yourself. Shame, anger, fatigue and sometimes deep sadness are normal after a great loss. Do not carry this alone: talk to your spouse, to a brother or sister, to a pastor you trust. If you can no longer sleep or eat, or if dark thoughts come back, see a doctor or a counselor without waiting. This is part of the rebuilding.

I am at the bottom, but I am not finished. I will count what I have left, then move forward.

2. Stopping and looking in the face

In the story of the lost son, the turning point is not the return to the father. It comes before: “when he came to himself” (Luke 15:17). The son looked his situation in the face. He saw where he was, he said it without lying to himself, then he decided: “I will get up and go to my father” (Luke 15:18).

Nehemiah did the same thing. When he arrives in Jerusalem, the city is in ruins. What does he do? He does not start to build. At night, he goes around the walls to see with his own eyes the state of things (Nehemiah 2:12-15). Only after that does he say to the people: “Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 2:17).

Before rebuilding, then, go around your ruins. Take a sheet of paper and answer honestly, in writing. What exactly happened? What was beyond my control? What did I do wrong: borrowed too much? mixed the business’s money with mine? depended on a single client? kept poor accounts? signed without reading? trusted without verifying? What will I never do again?

The goal is not to punish yourself. It is to learn. Write three lessons. They will be the foundations of your rebuilding. A bankruptcy from which nothing is learned is a total loss. One from which lessons are drawn becomes an experience that has no price.

lecons.titre: Rebuilding: counting what you have left and looking at the debts
lecons.html:
3. Counting what you have left

A widow comes to the prophet Elisha. Her husband is dead, she has debts, and the creditor wants to take her two sons as slaves. She is completely at the bottom. What does Elisha ask her? He does not just weep with her. He asks her a question: what do you have in the house? She answers that she has nothing, except a small jar of oil (2 Kings 4:1-2). And it is with this small jar that God will change everything.

This question is yours today: what do you have in the house? Almost always, we have more than we think, but we have never counted it. Take a big sheet and make four columns.

What I have

The money that remains, in the bank, in cash, in the tontine, in savings. The goods you still own: land, vehicle, motorbike, equipment, stock. What others owe you: clients who have not yet paid. Note the realistic value of each thing, not the one you hope for.

What I owe

All your debts, without hiding a single one: to whom, how much, since when, with what interest, by what date, with what guarantee. This is the column that frightens the most, and it is the one that frees you the fastest, because you only attack well what you know.

What I know how to do

Your skills, your experience, your degrees, your training. Do not forget what you know how to do with your hands. And do not forget what the fall taught you. If you ran a business, you know how to negotiate, organize, sell, lead people. This is worth money, even on the day the till is empty.

Those who are with me

Your family, your faithful friends, former clients who still respect you, former employees, honest suppliers, brothers and sisters from church, a possible mentor. Not all have left: “A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.” (Prov 17:17)

Then make the total: what I have, minus what I owe. The result is perhaps negative. It does not matter. It is your real starting point, and you only build on a real starting point. A traveler who does not know where he is cannot plot his route. You will fill in the sheet at the end of this chapter.

4. Looking at the debts in the face

Debts are the heaviest burden of someone who has gone bankrupt. “the borrower is servant to the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). But the Bible also says that uprightness consists in repaying: “The wicked borrow, and don’t pay back” (Psalm 37:21). Your goal is therefore to pay, honestly, at a pace you can keep. Here is how.

List everything, and put things in order. First put the debts that can take the essentials from you (housing, an item indispensable to your work), then those with a very high interest, then the others.

Go to your creditors before they come to you. Hiding makes everything worse. Tell the truth: here is my situation, here is what I can pay each month, here is my proposal. A creditor often prefers to receive a little, regularly, rather than nothing at all. Ask for the agreement to be written, with the amounts and dates.

Do not pay a debt with another debt. Flee loans with huge interest, moneylenders, “miracle solutions”. They turn a problem into a catastrophe.

Keep enough to live on. Before repaying, food, rent, health and the children’s school must be assured. An honest creditor will understand this.

Take advice. In the countries of the OHADA area, of which Benin is a part, the law provides procedures for businesses in difficulty: some serve to prevent the cessation of payments, others to organize the recovery or closure of the business. Consult a lawyer or a legal adviser to know what applies to your case, before making a big decision.

lecons.titre: Rebuilding: reducing, deciding and making a plan
lecons.html:
5. Reducing, selling, protecting

The time of rebuilding is not that of the lifestyle you had before. You need a survival budget: list every expense, separate the essential from the superfluous, and cut the superfluous without mercy. Outings, subscriptions, the big phone, the ceremonies where you spend to show that you are still somebody. Living in smaller housing, changing neighborhoods, selling the big vehicle: it is not a shame, it is wisdom. Pride costs a great deal to someone at the bottom, because it keeps the appearance and loses the essential.

Sell what produces nothing, to keep what can produce. The luxury vehicle can go. The motorbike, the equipment or the tool that will serve to earn your living must stay.

Also protect your household. Talk to your spouse, hiding nothing from them. Tell the children, according to their age, that the situation is difficult but that the family stands together. Many households break up after a bankruptcy, not because of money, but because of silence. Move forward together, by common agreement: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3)

6. Deciding where you want to go

When you know where you are, you can decide where you are going. This is where many go wrong: they want to get back exactly what they had, and quickly. Ask yourself these questions instead. What do I really want in a year? in three years? in ten years? Do I want to relaunch the same activity, or something else? What income do I need to live decently, then to repay? What am I ready to do, and no longer to do? What does my inventory really allow me to do? Write down the answers: “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it” (Habakkuk 2:2).

In general, there are three paths, which can be combined.

Finding a job again

A regular salary is the fastest basis for stabilizing, paying debts and catching your breath. Your experience is an asset. Accept not to resume at the level where you were: you can climb back. Refer to the parts “Securing a job” and “Moving up in your job”.

Relaunching a small activity

With what you have and what you know how to do, start small: an activity without premises, without big stock, without a loan. Do not despise the day of small beginnings. Someone who led twelve employees can very well start again alone. Those who bounce back do not always resume where they fell.

Doing both

This is often the best path: a salary that pays the needs and the debts, and a small activity alongside that grows. It is the “bridge” we spoke of in the part on career change.

A principle for choosing: rebuild stronger, not identically. Take your three lessons again. If the fall came from loans, the new activity will be done without a loan at first. If it came from dependence on a single client, you will have several clients. If it came from mixing the accounts, you will separate the money from day one. The parts on business management and on investing will give you the tools.

7. Making a plan

“The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit” (Proverbs 21:5). And Jesus asks: “For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost?” (Luke 14:28). You now have everything you need: your inventory, your lessons, your direction. Write the plan in three stages, with dates.

The stageWhat I am looking forWhat I do
Stabilize (the first 3 months)Have an income, even a small one, and stop the fall.Make my survival budget. List my debts. Meet each creditor. Find a first income: a job or a small activity.
Relaunch (from 3 months to 1 year)Earn regularly and start repaying.Keep the agreed repayments. Set aside a small amount each month, even a very small one. Train where I am missing something. Make known what I know how to do.
Rebuild (from 1 to 3 years)Repay the essential, have safety savings, and grow.Finish or almost finish the debts. Save at least three months of expenses. Grow the activity or move up in position. Think about investing, with caution.

Put a date and a figure on each stage: “In three months, I have an income of…”. A plan without a date is a wish. Review it each month, adjust it, but do not abandon it. And choose right now a first step, a very small one, to take this week.

lecons.titre: Rebuilding: trust, pitfalls and an example
lecons.html:
8. Rebuilding trust

A bankruptcy damages trust: that of creditors, clients, family, sometimes your own. Trust is rebuilt through small promises kept. Say what you are going to do, and do it on the day: a small payment on the promised date is worth more than a big promise. Give news before you are asked for it. Never lie, even to save face: today’s lie is tomorrow’s bankruptcy.

Also put things in order with God. Do not lose months looking for whether your fall is a punishment, an attack or a simple accident. Job’s friends spent their time looking for the fault, and God proved them wrong (Job 42:7). Ask him instead what he wants you to learn, and what he asks you to do now. If there is a fault to confess, confess it. If there is a repair to make, make it. Then move forward. God knows how to restore what the bad years have devoured (Joel 2:25), but he often does it through your work, and not in place of your work.

9. The pitfalls of someone at the bottom

The shortcut. When you are desperate, you are ready to believe anything: the investment that doubles in a month, the “brother” who knows the big deal, the pyramid, gambling, the easy loan. You have already lost once. Do not lose the little you have left. Refer to the warning signs in the part on investing.

The withdrawal. Shame pushes you to hide, to stop answering the phone, to stop going to church. It is the worst time to isolate yourself.

The accusation. Spending your days blaming the partner, the State, the client, fate. Even if you are right, it does not fill the till.

The big comeback. Wanting to start again big, with a big loan, to “catch up on everything”. It is often how you fall a second time.

Waiting for a miracle. Praying is essential, but prayer does not replace work: “He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand” (Proverbs 10:4). Pray, then get up.

10. An example (invented story)

Maurice runs a wholesale hardware store, with twelve employees. He bought a lot of stock on credit. His biggest client, a public works company, owes him a very large sum and has not paid for eight months. The suppliers and the bank demand their money. In less than a year, he closes the store, sells his big house and moves into a rental with his wife and their three children.

For a month, he hides: he no longer answers the phone and avoids church. One evening, his wife tells him: “Sit down, we are going to count.” On a sheet, he notes what he has: a motorbike, a van, a little equipment, two million that clients still owe him, a perfect knowledge of building materials and some forty clients who know him. Then he notes what he owes: eighteen million, of which nine to the bank, six to suppliers and three to individuals.

He goes to see each creditor. The bank accepts a five-year schedule. Two suppliers accept small monthly payments. He sells the van and keeps the motorbike. He finds a job as a stock manager in the store of a former competitor. On the side, he delivers small orders by motorbike to former clients, without stock and without a loan.

After eighteen months, he has repaid nearly a third of his debts and set aside three months of expenses. After four years, he reopens a small depot. This time, the accounts are separate, he buys on credit only what he can pay, and he has several clients instead of one. (The figures are there just to give an example.)

To sum up

Being at the bottom is not being finished. Before rebuilding, go around your ruins: understand what happened, without accusing yourself of everything and without excusing yourself of everything. Count what you have left: what you have, what you owe, what you know how to do, and those who support you. Face your debts with honesty, by going to your creditors and taking advice. Reduce your expenses and protect your household. Decide where you want to go, without trying to resume identically: rebuild stronger. Make a plan in three stages with dates: stabilize, relaunch, rebuild. Keep your small promises to regain trust. Flee shortcuts and scams. And pray, then get up: “When I fall, I will arise.”

titre: M14.2 — Wealth Creation: Growing and Getting Back Up
objectifs: ✦  You know how to move up in your job, and to build a bridge rather than jump if another path calls you.
✦  You know how to calculate a price, read a cash flow, invoice, get paid and formalize.
✦  You know how to invest with understanding, and to recognize a scam before putting in a franc.
✦  You know how to count what you have left, look your debts in the face and make a rebuilding plan if you fall, or protect yourself before the fall.

qcm.q: When your salary rises, what does the module’s rule say?
c: I immediately buy myself what I want
I first set aside at least half of the raise (savings, debt or investment) and I live on the rest
I do not change my way of spending and I set nothing aside
I set aside a tenth of the raise
qcm.e: The people who build wealth are not always those who earn the most: they are those who keep the most.

c: You leave your job as soon as the calling is felt
You never change paths
You leave one source of income only when another can replace it
You launch by going into debt to go faster
qcm.e: A bridge, not a leap: you keep one foot on the bank as long as the other side is not safe.

qcm.q: Among the criteria for leaving your job, which one is NOT part of them?
c: An activity that earns regularly for at least six months, at least half of the salary
An emergency savings of at least six months of minimum to live on
A spouse and family informed and in agreement
A boss who refused a raise
qcm.e: The five criteria: regular income, emergency savings, no heavy debt that depends on the salary, family in agreement, real clients. It is better that all are met.

qcm.q: What is rule number one of managing a small business?
c: Separate the business’s money from your own: separate account, fixed salary
Lend the till to the family in case of need
Set your prices by copying your neighbors
Write nothing to save time
qcm.e: The business is not your wallet. If you take anything other than your salary, note it with the date, the amount and the reason: it will be an advance to be repaid.

qcm.q: A bottle of juice costs 450 F in variable costs and sells for 800 F; fixed costs are 60,000 F per month. What is the break-even point?
c: About 75 bottles per month
About 133 bottles per month
About 172 bottles per month
About 600 bottles per month
qcm.e: Margin per bottle: 800 − 450 = 350 F. Break-even: 60,000 ÷ 350 ≈ 172. Below that, you lose money; above it, you earn.

qcm.q: You sold 1,000,000 F this month, but your clients paid only 600,000 F, and you have 700,000 F of expenses to pay. What happens?
c: All is well: the turnover is 1,000,000 F
You are short of cash, even if the business is “profitable”
You made 300,000 F of profit
The clients are not concerned
qcm.e: Turnover is not what you earn, and cash flow is the money actually available. Money often goes out before it comes in: ask for a deposit and follow up.

qcm.q: What does the module say about the 18% VAT?
c: It is your money, you can keep it
It concerns only large foreign companies
It is paid by the client and passed on to the State; never charge it if you are not entitled to
It is part of your profit
qcm.e: A business subject to the TPS that has not chosen the real regime cannot charge VAT. Have your situation confirmed by an accountant or by the DGI.

qcm.q: What must be settled before investing a single franc?
c: Nothing: the sooner the better
A travel insurance
A stock exchange account
No more expensive debt, emergency savings of at least three months, basic insurance, and a goal with a duration
qcm.e: Paying off a debt at 2% a month pays more than any serious investment. Golden rule: never borrowed money, nor money needed for food, rent or school fees.

qcm.q: How does an individual buy shares on the BRVM?
c: Directly on the stock exchange, on the Internet
By going through an approved SGI, with a securities account, after verifying its approval and comparing the fees
From any friend who knows someone
By sending the money to a Mobile Money number
qcm.e: An individual cannot buy directly on the stock exchange. Ask for the full rate schedule before opening an account.

qcm.q: Before buying land, what precaution does the module recommend?
c: Pay quickly in cash to get a good price
Trust the seller if he is a brother from church
Verify the seller’s right through a notary, go through a registered deed, pay by transfer and keep a receipt
Buy alone so as not to share the deal
qcm.e: A seller who rushes you is often trying to hide something. No cash without a deed, and never alone.

qcm.q: Which of these signs should alert you, as in the ICC Services affair?
c: A term deposit at fixed interest in an approved bank
An approved SGI that gives you its written rates
A return of 5.7% a year announced by the State for three years
A promise of huge and quick gain, “guaranteed”, and a commission for recruiting other people
qcm.e: “There is no huge and safe gain.” Religious trust does not excuse you from verifying: faith is shared, financial trust is verified.

qcm.q: What does the module say about cryptocurrencies?
c: They are regulated and guaranteed by the Central Bank
It is not a currency and it is not regulated: no protection if you are deceived or hacked, so extreme caution
They are ideal for doubling your money quickly
They replace the bank account
qcm.e: If you touch them despite everything: never borrowed money, never emergency or rent money, a very small part, a sum you accept to lose entirely. If you do not understand, do not touch them.

qcm.q: According to the part “Rebuilding”, where is the first battle of someone who falls from high fought?
c: Before the creditors
In the head: rejecting the sentence “it is over for you”
Before the court
In the search for a big loan
qcm.e: “A righteous man falls seven times, and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). What makes the difference between people is not the fall, it is getting back up.

qcm.q: What does Nehemiah do on arriving in Jerusalem, before saying “let’s rebuild”?
c: He launches the works right away
He goes around the walls at night to see the real state of things
He asks the king for money
He waits for God to act alone
qcm.e: Before rebuilding, you go around your ruins: what happened, what was beyond my control, what did I do wrong? The goal is not to punish yourself, it is to learn.

qcm.q: What are the four columns of the inventory to make when you have lost everything?
c: What I have, what I owe, what I know how to do, those who are with me
My friends, my enemies, my debts, my regrets
My salary, my rent, my expenses, my savings
My mistakes, my excuses, my projects, my dreams
qcm.e: Elisha’s widow had only a small jar of oil: the question “what do you have in the house?” is ours. Then you make the total (what I have minus what I owe), which is the real starting point.

qcm.q: What to do facing your creditors?
c: Hide until they forget
Go to them before they come, tell the truth, propose a realistic payment and have it written
Repay a debt with a new loan at high interest
Promise them everything to have peace
qcm.e: A creditor often prefers to receive a little, regularly, rather than nothing. Do not pay a debt with another debt, and keep enough to live on before repaying.

qcm.q: In the survival budget, what must be sold and what must be kept?
c: Sell the work tool, keep the luxury vehicle
Sell what produces nothing, keep what can produce (the motorbike, the equipment, the tool)
Sell everything
Sell nothing to keep up appearances
qcm.e: Pride costs a great deal to someone at the bottom: it keeps the appearance and loses the essential.

qcm.q: What are the three stages of the rebuilding plan?
c: Stabilize (first 3 months), relaunch (from 3 months to 1 year), rebuild (from 1 to 3 years)
Borrow, invest, repay
Wait, pray, start again identically
Hide, rest, take revenge
qcm.e: At each stage, put a date and a figure. A plan without a date is a wish. Review it each month.

qcm.q: What principle does the module give for choosing where to go after a bankruptcy?
